utterances.text: I don't know anything bad that I could say. You ask me, what is this bad thing that Mr. Seselj ever did? I'm not aware of any such thing. I just know that he's been here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: You've already indicated to us and confirmed that you have some experience in not telling the truth before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never in my life did I lie. This happened under your pressure, your threats, and your promises; third countries, et cetera. I left all of that, your money and everything. And also I confirmed that this is the very first time I see Mr. Seselj in person. Do you understand that? This is the very first time I see him in person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one could go anywhere. You have your own people everywhere. The cathedral in Subotica, that it was blown up, 50 metres' high, the cathedral is. And I was asked to confirm that? That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I can see that I'm not getting much in the way of answers from you, so I'll move on. I would like to ask you a few questions in relation to your first statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in July of 2002. And it's my understanding that you included in that statement that you will testify only if you feel that your personal and family safety would not be endangered. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what the investigator said right away, that I would be granted personal and family safety, and other things, change of identity and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So your family safety and your own safety was the subject of discussion between you and the investigators; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Those were their words. They said that my family wouldn't be endangered. My family wasn't in danger, and I was not endangered either. I don't know from which side you thought the danger would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: From the time of your first contact with the Prosecution Office in 2002 until the present time, have you ever been concerned about your own safety or the safety of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the truth is that the Prosecution contacted me through Natasa Kandic, not the other way 'round, and I explained how it all transpired. As for the safety of my family, it was never in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd like to perhaps refresh your memory on a couple of things and take you back to October of 2002, in a meeting that you had with some of the investigators. Is it not true that you reported that a week after you had met with members of the Prosecution Office, that Mr. Seselj spoke in Parliament in Belgrade about an ex-policeman that gave a statement to the Tribunal? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that information, and I doubt that Mr. Seselj would say something like that in the Parliament of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you recall, then, again with a view to refreshing your memory, advising the investigators that two or three days after Mr. Seselj made this comment in Parliament, that shots were fired at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true. I can tell you what really happened, and you can find it in my statement. First, Mr. Paolo took me to Novi Sad, wrote a statement on his laptop, but I didn't sign it. Then for three days Mr. Paolo and another German gentleman - I can't remember his name anymore - dictated it. Then I was sent back home. And it is true that in the evening, somebody fired a burst of fire from an automatic weapon, but I think that it has something to do with you, not with Mr. Seselj. That was a way of intimidating me, because first they said I would be indicted, I would be jailed if I didn't testify as they wanted me to do, and finally these shots were fired. On the 9th of January, a vehicle appeared with the passport, and I was on my way to Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So you saw this as an active intimidation on someone's part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And is it not also true that as a result of that, you told the investigators that you felt particularly vulnerable and feared for your safety because of your co-operation with the Tribunal, and you feared intimidation and retaliation as a result of that co-operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not what I said, not in those words. Of course, if somebody fires at my house, normally, my family and I are in danger. However, who fired those shots, I don't know. If I had any suspicions about anyone, be it the Radicals or whoever, because I think that's what you're aiming at, I would have reported this to the police. But you had DOS in power at the time, who were allies of yours. But I am sure that nobody from the Serbian Radical Party did that. I am 100 per cent sure, just as I'm sure that it was your doing, that it was the way of intimidating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: You kept one of the bullets that was fired, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were between 15 and 20 casings. One bullet penetrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And you kept one of the bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It stood there for a couple of days. But since I didn't need it, I threw it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So just to be clear, then, on your evidence: Despite what you said earlier, on this occasion you did feel at risk and intimidated as a result of the shooting at your house; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you would have been concerned just as well if your house had been shot at by somebody, and you would be concerned about your family. But I'm telling you, again, who I think it was who did it, who orchestrated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I don't know why you're so reluctant to say that you felt intimidated, and you asked me how I would feel. That's not in issue here. I want to know how you felt. Did you feel intimidated as a result of the shooting at your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say -- well, one thing is to be concerned, and the other thing is to be intimidated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. MacFarlane shouldn't demonstrate any anger against the witness. He is in the service of international justice, and his goal should be to find out the truth, not to achieve the desirable result in this proceedings for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I would like to turn to some material that's been already tendered in these proceedings in the form of excerpts from a book, and I have a few questions for you in relation to that. For the record, this is Exhibit 55J and 55K. I'm sorry, it's 55K and 55L. Thank you. My legal consultant has just reminded me. Sir, do you have both of those excerpts before you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And perhaps the Usher could assist you in directing your attention, firstly, to Exhibit 55K, and, in particular, the first page of 55K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to draw to your attention the first couple of paragraphs only. And do you see your name referred to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And in the first full paragraph, which sets out information concerning identification card, and date of birth, and so on, can you advise whether or not that information accurately describes you and identifies you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does. That was my residential address at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: What about the other information, in terms of occupation, your ethnic affiliation, your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a few more questions, sir. In between the two statements that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, one in July of 2002, one in November of 2002 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: -- given the improprieties that you told us about, why did you go back the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a problem with the interpretation. First, we have an interpreter stopping, finding the right word. The other one is trying to whisper something to her. And I believe that they should repeat this whole statement once again. I'm talking about the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be simpler if I asked the question again and provided an opportunity for the witness to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: We know that you met with the investigators with the Prosecution Office in July of 2002 and November of 2002, so several months went by in between those two statements. Given the improprieties that you talked to us about, why did you go back a second time to meet with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was invited to come to Belgrade in the same manner, because I was told I had to come. You're asking me why, but look here, I have been blackmailed with a fine of 100.000 dinars should I fail to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that a bit. You are an experienced policeman. You know that what they were talking about was the penalty for contempt. Why do you characterise that as blackmail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a blackmail on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: To outline the consequences of not telling the truth was blackmail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was supposed to tell the truth that would suit you. Then everything would be all right. However, if I told the real truth, then probably an indictment would have followed, as I had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: When the Chamber advised you of the consequences of not telling the truth at the beginning of your evidence, would you see that as blackmail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm glad to be here today to tell the truth. I'm repeating that once again. I could tell you a lot more things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you respect this Tribunal and its process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I respect this Tribunal? No. And these proceedings have all been engineered, particularly in the case of Serbs, and I stand by that. This is an arm of the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: If I might just have a moment, Your Honour, to check my notes. I believe I've completed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. MacFarlane doesn't have enough questions of his own, he may use my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It's quite all right. I have quite good notes here. I believe that completes my questioning. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I came here with regard to the disclosure of identity and, of course, to tell you the truth. I really don't understand why you're reluctant to take these documents that contain irrefutable facts, the statements of the 12th of August and the one from the April, and the fact that I was forced, with the threat of fine, to do this. I brought all these documents with me; also, an expert report of 10th of June. And I revealed my identity in all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said about the last date, 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The interpreters are requesting that you repeat the last statement that you made, the last -- not the entirety, but the very last portion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we spoke about the revealing of the identity, I said that I brought an original statement of the 19th of April, 2008, which was certified by a Novi Sad court. I voluntarily disclosed my name and all the other particulars. Then I have a statement from 12th of August, 2008, your directive for my health to be examined, on pain of a fine to be imposed on me. So I have all my documents with me. Since I revealed my identity to the public on the 19th of April in the media, I would kindly ask you to acquit Mr. Seselj of this, because he had nothing to do with that. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hall, I would like to pose a number of additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the documents to which the witness has just alluded, were you seeking their admission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the documents that the witness is talking about have already been published in the book that I am being tried for. The Usher has just given us these two statements that he gave to my associates. However, should you need an original, with the signature and the stamp of certification by the Court in Novi Sad, you may have it. But since the Prosecutor did not contest the authenticity of this document, it is up to you to decide. You may take it, and, then again, you may not or you needn't. I am here, being tried on the grounds that these are the particular documents that I published. I never published any Prosecution documents. All I published were the statements given by this witness to my associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't exactly answer my question, Mr. Seselj. If you wish to tender those documents as part of your Defence, and make such use of them as you would like to do so, that's entirely a matter for you. But the documents really ought to come through counsel or, in your case, self-representing accused, rather than through the witness, himself. It's entirely a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't think it necessary to tender them. If you would like to have them in evidence, then take it that as of now, I am tendering them into evidence, because nobody has challenged the authenticity of the documents that I published in the book that I am being tried for. This is an answer to your question. I don't know if I'm being interpreted correctly or whether that created a kind of confusion. So what I published in my book was never challenged by Mr. MacFarlane as the statements given by this witness to my Defence team. And I'm not talking about this witness only. I'm talking about all the 10 witnesses. I hope I was a bit clearer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I hear perfectly what you're saying, Mr. Seselj, but it's not for the Court to request evidence. It's for a party to the proceedings to submit it for the Court if they think it's going to assist in the determination of the matters that the Court has to decide. If there's doubt in the matter, my advice to you would be to tender them. That's entirely a matter for you, still.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will heed your advice, because I think it is a benevolent one. But I'm now facing technical problems, because whenever I want something to tender into evidence, I have to provide a copy to the OTP, to you. Probably, a translation would be needed. But in this particular case, everything has been translated, all the statements stated and quoted if this book have been translated, everything exists in the English, and nobody challenged the fact that these witnesses, indeed, gave these statements. And let's cut this whole story short. I would like to tender this into evidence, if you would accept it, although had I really been interested in doing so, I would have provided copies to you and the OTP in good time. But I didn't consider that important enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, what's really important, of course, is that the information contained in the statements is before the Court. If you are satisfied that it is already, and you feel that it's simply duplicating matters, then my advice may not be as pertinent as it otherwise would be. I think you see what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have already accepted your advice. Therefore, the Usher can take these documents from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, did you have a view, before the Chamber formally admits -- decides whether to admit these documents as an exhibit? Have you seen them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I was invited to by the witness. I haven't seen them, so I'm not sure what the contents are. I don't have a particular view one way or the other. If Mr. Seselj wishes to tender them and rely upon them, then I'm not objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seselj, you have a right to re-examine the witness, and I would remind you that re-examination is not an opportunity to re-open your case in chief, but it must be confined to matters arising out of the questions that the side opposite - in this case, Mr. MacFarlane - asked in cross-examination. So you may begin your re-examination now. And I would inform the parties that because, as is well known, we could not sit continuously until 7.00, when the Court rises for the day, we intend to break at 5.35 for 20 minutes and then resume at 5.55 for the final session of the day. So you may begin. You have another six minutes before the break, Mr. Seselj, to begin your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will exclusively be dealing with the questions asked by Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first question concerns the shooting in front of your house. Is it true that this burst of fire was fired in front of your house while you were being interrogated in Belgrade or in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So did that happen before your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that nobody in the Serbian public had any idea that you were being proofed to appear as a witness in the Milosevic case, or in my case, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that the reason why you established a link between this shooting with the Prosecution or people co-operating with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. The first question: Do you know that the Serbian public intensively followed the proceedings of Slobodan Milosevic, as well as my own trial, because there was direct TV coverage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the Serbian public, beforehand and now, was there a lot of talk about many Prosecution witnesses providing false testimony here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware of any example that anyone in The Hague Tribunal testified in any case against accused Serbs as a Prosecution witness, and that such a person later had some kind of trouble in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You do not know of any example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't heard of any, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm interested in this question of oath. I think that your answer was a bit clumsy, your answer provided to the friend of the Court. Do you know that in the legal system of Serbia and the former Yugoslavia, an oath never existed in the legal system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I answered, as a policeman. He didn't understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think that you were not clear enough, and that's why I wanted to make it clear. Is it correct that in the 1990s and for decades before that, when a witness appeared in court, the only thing that would happen would be that the judge would caution him or her that they have to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And to say that they will be criminally liable if they perjure themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did that mean that there was no oath whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accused is leading the witness to an extreme. He might as well take the witness stand himself. He's placing all of the evidence and information that he wants into the mouth of the witness. I've restrained myself from objecting before, but this is extreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seselj, you take Mr. MacFarlane's point that this is your witness. You can't lead him. You can't ask questions in such a way that suggests the answer. Ask him a question and let him give the information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hall, this witness is not a lawyer. He is a policeman, yes, but he could not express himself consistently, from a legal point of view. However, any lawyer in Serbia knows that until a few years ago, we never had the institute of witnesses taking oath before testifying. This was introduced only seven or eight years ago, ten maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're giving evidence, Mr. Seselj. Ask the witness the question in such a way that he testifies from his own knowledge and experience.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyone in Serbia and in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, do they have any kind of regard for that kind of oath when they say, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, and nothing but the truth? Or, to put it very simply, does anyone consider that to be a real oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As a policeman, I know that there is no oath. The judge does orally caution a witness that he or she has to tell the truth so that criminal charges would not be brought against them, but there is no oath of this kind when I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't understand my question this time. There is a solemn oath before The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me explain the essence of my question to you now. And it says: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." Does anyone from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, not only Serbia, but all of the former Yugoslavia, consider that to be an oath, in the true sense of word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it the same thing when you say, I solemnly declare, or if you say, I swear that I shall speak the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was the essence of my question. So does that mean that a person who says, I solemnly declare, does not believe that he has sworn an oath at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Also, you mentioned in one of your answers given to Mr. MacFarlane this fear of yours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, since you're going on to something else. This would be the time that we would take the break, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In response to my last question, you said that no one in the territory of the former Yugoslavia took the solemn declaration at the ICTY as an oath. Does that mean, simultaneously, that whoever perjures himself after giving this solemn declaration does not think that he has actually perjured himself, provided false evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's a bad thing, what I did in the Slobodan Milosevic case, but I was forced to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am not asking you about that. It is obvious from your entire statement that you were forced to do so. But you confirmed that the public believes that there were many false witnesses who appeared here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Some of those who said, I solemnly declare, et cetera, et cetera, and then provided false evidence, do they believe that they committed perjury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They believe that they did not commit perjury. You mentioned 2005 as well in one of your answers to Mr. MacFarlane. You said that that was a cut-off year. You said the 1st of January, 2005. Was that a mistake? Did you mean the 31st of December, 2005?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant, but from the 1st of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did that pertain to the date from which it was no longer possible to issue new indictments in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that something that made you relax, in terms of these pressures from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can that be a reason why many other potential witnesses of the Prosecution gave up on testifying and many of them joined my Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You believe that that is the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. I think that they were all blackmailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're leading the witness again, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Hall, I've just completed my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we release --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Before the witness is released, have you taken a decision on these documents that he wished to volunteer? Before you answer that, let me put you fully in the picture. If they aren't yet translated into one of the two working languages of the Tribunal, French and English, if your application is to have them admitted, they could only be marked for identification at this stage. But have you made a decision, before we release the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took Mr. Morrison's advice, Mr. Hall, and I thought that I can formally tender it now. I'm sure that it was translated years ago into the English language, because it was part of my criminal complaint against Carla Del Ponte. Another friend of the Court is looking at that criminal complaint. He was appointed about a year ago, and he is supposed to complete his work by the 7th of October this year. So there is a translation into English. There is a translation of all the text from the book into English. And then I suggest that the Registry this for you so that it can be admitted into evidence. Frankly, I didn't have it translated because I was sure that it had been translated a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would mark them for identification and give them an exhibit number with that MFI qualification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 55J becomes D2, MFI'd. And 55L -- witness documents become D2, MFI'd, and D3, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also suggest that this witness's statement that I handed over to you, according to Rule 65 ter, in a preliminary way, be admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court Officer has alerted the Chamber that some of these documents name witnesses, so the documents would be admitted under seal. Yes. There was something else you wished to say, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just suggested that this preliminary statement given by this witness, in view of his appearance in these proceedings, that I submitted to you in accordance with Rule 65 ter, that you admit that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have had the oral testimony of the witness, and that is all that the Chamber requires. Mr. Witness, we thank you for your attendance before the Tribunal. You are released. I believe because of the protective measures, we would have to lower the shades in order for you to be escorted from the courtroom. You wish to say something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just as I said, this is my request: to reject this indictment against Vojislav Seselj. As soon as I go back to Serbia, and that's another matter, I'm going to present my identity once again, I'm going to make it known. I don't need these code-names, pseudonyms, whatever. I have a name, I have my family.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to the interpretation. Mr. Hall, you said "oral testimony," and the interpreter said "oralno svedocenja." It cannot be translated that way, it can only be translated "verbalno svedocenja," because "oralno svedocenja" in Serbian does not exist. Tablets can be taken orally, but testimony can only be verbal, or viva voce, as one says in Latin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, let me correct myself for the ease of the interpretation and the consistency of the two languages. We have the viva voce testimony of the witness. Thank you, Mr. Seselj. So the witness may be escorted from the room once the blinds are lowered. Mr. Seselj, do I correctly understand that your next witness, there are no protective measures, if I'm looking at the order correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, no protective measures are needed for him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call Hadzi Zoran Drazilovic as the next Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good evening to you, sir. Can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration on the card that the Usher has now handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. First of all, I would point out that the solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony before this Tribunal. And should you fail to do so, this Tribunal is empowered, under the Statute which created it, to impose penalties for perjury; that is, for false or misleading testimony. Would you begin by telling us your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zoran Drazilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, and what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 19th of May, 1947, and I'm a retired army officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been called in these proceedings by Mr. Seselj, who is at your left, and he will begin by asking questions of you, after which Mr. MacFarlane, who appears as Amicus Prosecutor, would have the right to cross-examine you on matters arising out of your testimony-in-chief. And then Mr. Seselj would have a right to re-examine you. And the Judges may, at that point, or, indeed, at any earlier point, have their own questions of you, arising out of what the parties have said. Because of the time of day, I should alert you that in the unlikely event that your testimony is not completed today, because the Court would rise for the day at 7.00, it would continue at 2.30 tomorrow afternoon. And I invite Mr. Seselj to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Drazilovic, I have noted in the details that your name has changed in the meantime. Your name now is Hadzi Zoran Drazilovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But because that name is written in my old passport, that is why I introduced myself in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You acquired this religious title?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you have been very much devoted lately to religion, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I've been a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement from its very induction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what about the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: From the day it was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you perform any particular duties in the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I was deputy chief for -- how is it called?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you perform any duties first in the Crisis and then the War Staff of the party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Drazilovic, I must point out to you that your evidence has to be interpreted. So before you attempt to answer the question that Mr. Seselj poses, or, for that matter, when Mr. MacFarlane's turn comes, allow a gap so that the interpreters can catch up. Yes, Mr. Seselj, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you deputy chief of the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: First, I was deputy chief for Logistics. And after Zoran Rankic resigned, I became chief for Logistics and deputy chief of the War Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While you were there, who was the chief?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the War Staff was Ljubisa Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After his resignation, did Zoran Rankic do anything on the staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: No, he had no duties, and he came to visit us maybe two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After his departure?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after his departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the reason for the Serbian Radical Party to establish a crisis staff? Can you please wait for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for the Serbian Radical Party to establish a crisis staff was the following: A large number of Serbs, whole families, had been expelled and were fleeing towards Serbia. They would arrive in Serbia, and our job was to receive them, to provide accommodation for them, to provide the basic necessities, such as food, footwear, clothes and medicine, and to try to enroll their children in various schools in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where were these Serbs fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: From Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who decided to set up a crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: The decision to set up a crisis staff was taken by the Serbian Radical Party or, rather, its main board.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff raise any funds?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: That was strictly forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Once the conflicts became widespread in this former Yugoslav federal unit, did the Crisis Staff perform any other duties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We started sending volunteers to the most endangered area. That was at the beginning. Most were the people who were born there or who had families in those regions. That was one of the jobs that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did we send them initially?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: They would go to - what's it called? - the Territorial Defence, and then the army accepted them and deployed them to certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the official name of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Abbreviated "JNA"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember exactly as of which date we started sending volunteers to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could it have been a bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened on the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: There was a horrendous plight in and out of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember the time when an immediate danger of war was declared; do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could it have been the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, because that is when the JNA received our volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who provided transportation for the volunteers to the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: At first, this was done by the people who were on the ground, and later on Croatia -- Serb associations from Croatia, and later from Bosnia-Herzegovina, were the ones who provided vehicles, and the provisional government of the Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when did the JNA start organising transport?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the MUP or the police of Serbia ever take part in the transportation of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the police did not participate in that. Those were mainly privately-owned buses provided by local civilians from the endangered territories, as well as the Serb associations from Croatia, the Serb association from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the provisional government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anyone from amongst the Serbian political or police officials of Serbia, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or Republika Srpska, come to the headquarters of the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Since I spent most of my time in the Crisis Staff, I never saw any officials or politicians coming there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you have your first contact with The Hague Prosecution Office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: My first contact with the OTP was immediately before you volunteered to be transferred to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did you talk to at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I talked -- Paolo Stocchi and Sabine Schulz. I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did it come about, these contacts? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: These contacts were established in the following manner: My brother called me and told me that there was an Italian looking for me, an Italian journalist - as he said, that's how he had introduced himself - and that he wished to interview me. We always associate interviews with journalists. I never thought that that could be an interrogation. In fact, I learned only later that that was not to be an interview with a journalist, but, in fact, the person looking for me represented The Hague Tribunal Prosecution Office. As a member of the Serbian Radical Party, I immediately went to the party HQ and reported to my president, Dr. Vojislav Seselj, and told him that I had been called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did I tell you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojislav Seselj told me the following, If they had invited you, you should come -- you should go there and give them truthful responses to whatever they ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how did these investigators treat you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: When I came, I reported at the gatehouse. I told them my name. They quickly came downstairs and took me to a small room, where there was a desk with a computer on it. Sitting at the desk was Paolo Stocchi. I sat opposite him, and on my right, Sabine Schulz sat, if I'm not mistaken. She kept quiet the whole time. She didn't ask me any questions, whereas the investigator, Paolo Stocchi, was very arrogant, and he started asking me questions -- or, rather, talking to me. And then he raised his voice at one point and told me that if I did not co-operate with him, I would be jailed for seven years or so and that I would have to pay an enormous amount of money as a fine. Something happened to me at that moment. I became frightened. I kept asking myself, Why would I go to jail, why do I have to pay a fine? It was obviously his attempt to intimidate him [as interpreted], and he was successful in doing so. Then he started asking me a whole lot of various questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of questions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: He asked me the following: He said that he did know, but he, nevertheless, invited me to come over and to confirm certain things for which I was allegedly informed about. There were a lot of mistaken dates or wrong names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he ask you anything about Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you remember what?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me about Western Slavonia. He was also rough in his attitude, because he said that if I didn't confirm what he knew was the truth, I would go to jail. He asked me about a group of - how was this group called? - yes, the White Eagles, who had allegedly went with us, according to him, to Western Slavonia. Since I was there every day, I couldn't really remember this group joining us, because any group or any individual, and I'm talking about volunteers, could have gone there under their own arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, was there any mention of people nicknamed Kvocka and Sikirica? Were those the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me if we had Kvocka and Sikirica among our volunteers, and I said, Yes, we do have Kvocka and Sikirica as our volunteers, but those were their nicknames; those were not their family names. Only a few years later, I realised that there were people from Republika Srpska with family names like that who were convicted in Bosnia. Sikirica was the man who got killed, and he was from the surrounds of Aleksinac, and Kvocka was from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Stocchi insist that you confirm that Kvocka was a policeman in Prijedor, and Sikirica, who was also convicted here, was from Prijedor as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he insisted on my confirming and admitting that those were our volunteers. He didn't say, for example, the real name of Kvocka. He exclusively referred to them by their nicknames. He only spoke of Kvocka, and he insisted, to which I said, yes, those were our volunteers, believing that he was talking, actually, about our volunteers who had these nicknames, as many of us did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Was there any discussion about the Detachment of Leva Supoderica in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Leva Supoderica was discussed too. He also insisted that I admit or confirm that the Leva Supoderica Unit was a unit of the Serb Radical Party. That unit did exist in Vukovar, and that unit consisted only of locals, people from that area that was called Leva Supoderica. That is an area in Vukovar. Later on, when our volunteers went to Vukovar, the army assigned them to different units, and some of our volunteers probably went to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he ask you about some Topola?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that many of us had nicknames. Some people had nicknames that showed the village or town or area that they were from. It is possible that there was a person nicknamed Topola. However, that man did not go to Western Slavonia through us, that is to say, to Vukovar. He probably came with a neighbour or friend who was on leave, and he went with him then. That happened often. When people went on leave, on furlough, neighbours and friends would often accompany such a person back into the field, and they'd stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there any reference to the rally of the Serb Radical Party in Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then he was rather rough and tough on me then. He was forcing me to confirm that the rally of the Serb Radical Party in Mali Zvornik was sometime in April - I cannot remember the exact date - of 1992. There was a rally of the Serb Chetnik Movement, but that was sometime in 1991; that is to say, much, much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Stocchi offer you anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Same basic issue as before; we're so far afield from the issues set out in the order in lieu of indictment that I don't understand why the accused continues to be so far afield. It's not even on the periphery. It's dealing with issues, perhaps, that might arise in his main trial, and I can't help but wonder if he is seeking to establish a record for purposes outside of these proceedings. In any event, I continue to object on the grounds of complete irrelevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the objection, as articulated by Mr. MacFarlane, it appears to us that you are so patently irrelevant that if this is the only testimony that you have to elicit from this witness, we would have no option but to prevent you leading further evidence, because it is of no assistance whatever to this Chamber, seized of the present matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Hall, you can do whatever you please, but I think that these matters are very important for the essence of this witness's testimony. This witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm certain that you think so, Mr. Seselj. But, of course, in the order of things, it is for the Chamber to rule on relevance. And what I am saying, and I would repeat myself, is that if you have no relevant evidence - by "relevant," I mean dealing with the order in lieu of indictment, which is the only thing with which this Chamber is concerned - then this witness cannot assist us. Do you have any relevant questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I continue to insist on all my questions being relevant, and I just have a few questions left. I will be done in five or six minutes, so bear with me. But if you don't have the patience to do that, then you can throw me out of this courtroom, too. I can just walk out of here, if you wish. But if you have given me five hours for presenting the Defence case, then let me use those five hours. Just imagine all the things that Mr. MacFarlane spoke about in his opening statement. These were matters that were totally irrelevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Proceed with your relevant questions, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My last question, which I would like to have answered, is whether Mr. Stocchi offered you anything.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Something very interesting was happening. Although he was so rough, and although his behaviour was so forceful, and these suggestive answers that he was -- suggestive questions that he was putting, trying to put answers into my mouth, he, nevertheless, tried to establish some kind of relationship of friendship with me. Now, what happened? A few very important things happened that -- how should I put this? I was in a very difficult situation. It affected me considerably, as a human being. It affected my life after that as well. He offered to be my friend. He said that he and I could go out together, that we could go to some hotel that had a restaurant that was called Pecina, the Cave, and that I should bring some girls there, and that that would be our friendship. That was the kind of friendship that he had offered to me. Another thing that he did was the following: At one point, he started saying that I was very wrong about all of this, that I trust my president, Dr. Vojislav Seselj, too much, so why am I saying that things are in a certain way when Mr. Vojislav Seselj does not trust me at all, does not have any kind of regard for me, and that, quite simply, I should accept what he was saying to me and that I should say some things -- or, rather, confirm some things that he had been saying all along; that he said that such and such a person had done such and such a thing. Of course, I refused that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you have your last contact with the representatives of The Hague OTP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was in 2007. 2007, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did you react then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I was asked then to report to the Office of the Prosecutor for War Crimes, and they are in my neighbourhood. I did show up there. And who was there? Christine Dahl. I don't want to make any mistakes. Yes. In some informal conversation that was an interrogation at the same time, she made me an offer. She said that I can set an amount, that I can say what I want. She offered that they would buy clothes for me. But the most important thing was that she insisted that I be a Prosecution witness, which I refused straight away, and I said that I could only be a witness for the Defence of Dr. Vojislav Seselj. She repeated that several times, but I said to her what I had to say and that I stood by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you officially talk to the members of the team assisting me and my defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was 2007, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many statements did you give to my associates?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't really want to make any mistakes. Two statements, two or three. I do apologise. I may have made a mistake, but it's two or three, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they certified in court, these statements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you give your consent to have these statements of yours used in public?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave my consent for all of these statements of mine to be used in public, and it was an honour for me to have Dr. Vojislav Seselj mention me in any book or whatever else was coming out in relation to all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you give your explicit consent for your statements to be published in my book? I don't want to mention the title of the book because they are going to move into closed session straight away.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat what I said. It was an honour for me to have your -- to have my name mentioned in your books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Again, I'm asking you: Did you give your explicit consent to have your name mentioned in my book?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you refuse to be a Prosecution witness in the proceedings against me, even on pain of a subpoena?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you refuse to be a Chamber witness in the proceedings against me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Trial Chamber ultimately give up on you testifying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the Trial Chamber in a dilemma as to whether they would press criminal charges against you or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, you're speeding up. The interpreters are having difficulty keeping up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'll speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the Trial Chamber in a dilemma as to whether they would press criminal charges against you because you refused to testify, or did they consider giving up altogether on your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: It's probably the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A dilemma is either one or the other thing. Did they ultimately give up on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's a rank leading question, and it calls for speculation by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know when protective measures were dismissed in respect of yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I think that happened four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When protective measures were introduced, did anyone notify you to the effect that protective measures would be introduced in your case, and did they ask you anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: No one informed me. No one asked for my consent for introducing protective measures. When I was being interrogated and after these interrogations, I did not receive a copy of anything, of anything that had been discussed with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you read those alleged statements of yours that you signed before The Hague investigators?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read them. It was usually five minutes before the questioning would be over. I would be so tired and so annoyed, quite simply out of control. Or, rather, they would let me read it, and that would be it. When I asked that they give me a copy of my own, they said that I was not entitled to one. Later on, I heard that I actually was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested in understanding --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested in having an understanding of the sequence of events here, so I'd like to take you through the sequence over a period of time. It's my understanding that you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in April of 2003, and that was your first statement to the OTP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I understand as well that you had quite a number of different types of contacts with investigators with the OTP over a period of time, perhaps as many as seven or eight; not necessarily leading to statements, but, rather, contacts and discussions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: How many contacts do you think you had with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I think from that date that you mentioned up until, say -- well, it went on for four or five days, four days, five days. I came every morning at 10.00, and we would be done sometime in the afternoon, after having taken a short lunch break as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Were there other occasions when you had meetings with investigators of the OTP, aside from that one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: After that, there was another call a year or two later - I cannot remember exactly - and, of course, this one in Belgrade four years ago, the one that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could refresh your memory a bit by referring you to a statement that you gave on the 24th of January of 2007, and see if you recall making this comment. You were talking about your contact with Paolo with the OTP, and you said: "I just know that they told me that they were taking me as their witness in the case against Vojislav Seselj. I found it strange that whenever I talked to someone from the party, the next day they would call me again for an interview. I tried to find out what they actually wanted from me, but I noticed that strange things were happening, and I had to take refuge in a monastery. But in the meantime, I visited them about seven to eight times." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRAZILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that statement. It is possible that I said that, but I really don't remember that. I did spend a lot of time at monasteries, but not seeking refuge. Refuge from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd like to refer the Chamber to an exhibit. It's Exhibit 55O, and we have copies here for the Chamber. This purports to be a statement given by the witness in August of 2008, prepared personally by him, but I'll ask him questions about that. Before I ask questions of the witness on the statement, I would ask that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we are about to take the adjournment until 2.30 tomorrow afternoon. And I would remind the witness that having been sworn as a witness in this matter, you not have any communication with counsel for the -- well, Mr. MacFarlane, on the one hand, or Mr. Seselj, on the other. And, indeed, in any conversation that you have outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we will continue tomorrow at 2.30.
